items.questionAndWhy: Does leadership that represents and builds a shared group identity relate to adolescents' identification with their team, commitment and wellbeing? This distinguishes leadership rooted in collective identity from authority based only on individual status.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers analyzed reports from 3,540 adolescent athletes in 395 sports teams across 11 countries. They examined coaches' and peer leaders' identity leadership, team identification, wellbeing and commitment, with comparisons across country, sex and ages 12–17.
items.whatTheyFound: Stronger perceived identity leadership was associated with stronger team identification, which in turn was associated with higher wellbeing and commitment. The reported pattern was broadly consistent across countries, boys and girls and age groups. The study is observational: its modeled indirect associations do not establish causal mediation or rule out favorable-team selection.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX organizational assessments could distinguish identity representation, identity building and group identification from leader charisma or formal authority. The study supports investigating these constructs across cultures, but transferring sport associations to military teams or influence campaigns requires experimental or longitudinal validation.
items.streamTitle: Identity leadership predicted team identification and functioning across 11 countries
items.streamSummary: A 3,540-athlete study in 395 teams across 11 countries linked coaches' and peers' identity leadership with team identification, wellbeing and commitment; the cross-cultural consistency is observational, not a causal intervention effect.
items.attribution: Butalia et al. — Scientific Reports (cross-national observational team study, November 13)

items.questionAndWhy: Does the ability to overcome one's privileged perspective and infer what a partner knows explain success in cooperative conversation beyond general attention or working memory? This identifies a measurable social-cognitive requirement for exchanging different information.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers studied 31 participants with recent right-hemisphere stroke and 16 matched controls. Participants cooperatively identified differences between pictures without seeing their partner's image, completed nonverbal false-belief tasks, and were assessed for attention and working memory.
items.whatTheyFound: In the published analysis, perspective-conflict theory-of-mind performance predicted conversational success (standardized beta 0.42, p=.023); adding false-belief reasoning increased model fit by about 0.115 in R-squared. The clinical sample was small, recruited during recovery, and excluded some patients unable to complete testing. Association does not establish a causal communication intervention.
items.whatItMeans: The concrete transferable construct is a person's ability to separate what they know from what a partner knows during collaborative information exchange. PSYWERX could test this in analyst teams using controlled information asymmetries; improvement in healthy operational populations has not been demonstrated.
items.streamTitle: Perspective-conflict reasoning predicted success in cooperative conversation after stroke
items.streamSummary: Among 31 right-hemisphere-stroke patients and 16 controls, partner-perspective reasoning predicted cooperative picture-description success beyond several cognitive controls. Small clinical observational data do not establish operational-team effects.
items.attribution: Suazo, Blake and Schnur — Scientific Reports (clinical social-cognition observational study, November 13)

items.questionAndWhy: Can interoperable data exchange and AI support shorten the time between sensor information and a human targeting decision across allied systems? The operational challenge is coordination through tactical, operational and strategic levels.
items.whatTheyDid: NATO ACT described a DiBaX26 trial involving operators from 11 Allies and headquarters organizations, working across five countries with over 6,000 simulated targets and more than 100 live targets. Operators would first complete a targeting cycle without AI support, then repeat it with AI-enabled tools and a common target-data model.
items.whatTheyFound: The stated objective was to cut information-to-decision time by more than half and assess cross-system data exchange, while keeping engagement decisions under human authority. The October 21 source describes planned tests and requirements; it does not report measured reductions, independent effects or a fielded operational capability.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX COA and human–AI decision assessment, this provides a concrete comparison design: record latency, information quality, inter-actor handoffs, human overrides and error rates under baseline and AI-supported conditions. The proposed performance target must not be reported as achieved.
items.streamTitle: NATO specified a baseline-controlled experiment on targeting decision latency
items.streamSummary: NATO ACT outlined a baseline-versus-AI test of allied targeting data exchange across 11 nations and thousands of simulated targets; its goal of halving decision latency was a target, not a published result.
items.attribution: NATO Allied Command Transformation — Next Generation Targeting at DiBaX26 (official experimentation plan, October 21)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a single multilingual language system label affect, psychological constructs, behavior and related language indicators while calibrating decisions and keeping unsupported classes visible?
items.whatTheyDid: The NALU framework combines a shared Transformer encoder, specialized prediction heads, supervision masks, calibration and an auditable interpretation layer. An initial stage used 205,109 samples; an expanded stage used 589,155 unique Portuguese and English records with twelve prediction heads.
items.whatTheyFound: The initial eight-head model reported a composite test score of 0.761, with 95% bootstrap interval 0.754–0.767. In the expanded setting, sentiment macro-F1 was 0.7912 and emotion macro-F1 0.6858. Calibration improved several heads but not the risk head significantly (p=.096). Classes with insufficient held-out positives were not claimed to be evaluated.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX text coding could compare multi-construct labels with qualified human annotation and inspect calibration separately by language and construct. The system predicts language-derived indicators, not actual beliefs, diagnosed conditions or causal psychological states; operational transfer needs independent validation.
items.streamTitle: Multilingual language model separated psychological labels while retaining unestimable classes
items.streamSummary: NALU evaluated a multilingual, multitask psychological-language classifier on 589,155 unique Portuguese/English records; performance differed by construct, with insufficiently supported classes explicitly treated as unestimable.
items.attribution: Diego Resende Faria — Scientific Reports (multitask language-classification study, November 13)

items.questionAndWhy: How can researchers distinguish plausible emergent social patterns from proposed micro-to-macro causal explanations inside an LLM-agent simulation?
items.whatTheyDid: The CAMO framework converts mechanistic hypotheses into computable features from simulator records, derives a compact explanatory graph around a target collective outcome, and uses simulator-internal counterfactual probes to orient uncertain connections. Authors evaluated four emergent simulation settings.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors report that the procedure generated compact hypothesized causal pathways and could update explanations when simulation probes contradicted them. These tests intervene within the simulated world; they do not independently establish human causal structure, forecast accuracy or valid interventions on real groups.
items.whatItMeans: The specific PSYWERX application is to connect agent-level decision traces to collective output changes and compare alternative mechanisms with matched simulator interventions. This April methods paper is included for its distinct architecture; empirical human validation remains essential.
items.streamTitle: CAMO probed causal explanations inside generative social simulations
items.streamSummary: CAMO builds causal candidate graphs from LLM-agent traces and tests them with simulator counterfactual probes in four emergent settings. It identifies simulated mechanisms, not independently verified human causal pathways.
items.attribution: Yu, Guo, Hou, Xue and Ma — arXiv CAMO preprint (simulation causal-discovery methodology, April 16)

items.questionAndWhy: Do LLM-agent architectures and explicit behavioral attitudes change modeled protective choices, and can agent responses be compared with human experimental benchmarks instead of assumed plausible?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers combined a contact-network epidemic model, LLM decision agents and human epigame data. Four agent architectures made dynamic quarantine choices during a 15-day simulation, with comparisons against a no-intervention baseline and a previous human epigame.
items.whatTheyFound: Simulated quarantine compliance peaked at about 58–65% on day six. Perceived severity predicted simulated quarantine choice (reported beta 0.33, p=.002), but explained little variation (pseudo-R-squared .055). Agent architecture influenced dynamics, and geographic labels alone did not produce consistent cultural differentiation without explicit attitudinal inputs. Comparisons to human data were limited.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX synthetic populations, explicitly vary behavioral-prior assumptions, model architecture and cultural attitudes rather than relying on country labels. This June work supplies a useful controlled human-comparison design, not validated intervention forecasts for epidemics or other operational domains.
items.streamTitle: Epi-LLM showed agent architecture and explicit attitudes shape modeled responses
items.streamSummary: Epi-LLM compared four LLM-agent architectures against epigame-related human evidence; simulated quarantine behavior varied with architecture and stated attitudes, while geographic labels alone did not ensure cultural fidelity.
items.attribution: Ferenz et al. — arXiv Epi-LLM preprint (behavioral agent-based simulation benchmark, June 1)

items.questionAndWhy: Can repeated measurements distinguish whether people recognize a claim, believe it, share it or act on it as the information environment changes rapidly?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers released four waves of surveys fielded February 4–11, 2020 in China during the early COVID-19 outbreak. The initial wave included 1,422 participants; 1,153 completed all four (81.1% retention). The data include facts, rumors, misinformation and actionable recommendations alongside individual-difference measures.
items.whatTheyFound: The primary finding is the availability of a documented repeated-measures dataset, not an estimated misinformation-treatment effect. It distinguishes familiarity, perceived accuracy, sharing or willingness to share, and execution or willingness to act across waves. Attrition, self-report, pandemic context and the narrow collection window constrain generalization.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete research asset for PSYWERX to compare distinct cognitive and behavioral outcome measures over time and assess within-person variability. Longitudinal associations do not by themselves identify causal misinformation effects; any transfer to other contexts needs validation.
items.streamTitle: Four-wave misinformation dataset separated familiarity, accuracy, sharing and action
items.streamSummary: A new public dataset follows 1,153 of 1,422 initial Chinese participants across four February 2020 waves, separating claim familiarity, perceived accuracy, sharing and action measures. It is research infrastructure, not a causal misinformation result.
items.attribution: Chen, Zhang, Zhu and Xie — Scientific Data (public longitudinal data descriptor, November 13)

items.questionAndWhy: Can AR deliver virtual warm/cool sensations while preserving fingertip dexterity and the ability to perceive real surface temperatures?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built a palm-mounted thermal device that preserves fingertip contact, senses and re-renders physical surface temperature, and delivers spatially and temporally varying thermal patterns. Human-subject experiments compared indirect and moving feedback designs.
items.whatTheyFound: Tests indicated that indirect palm cues preserved comfort and immersion but reduced realism when visually implied contact occurred at the fingertips. Thermal passthrough supported discrimination between physical and rendered temperature, and moving patterns increased reported realism and immersion compared with static feedback. This is prototype-level evaluation, not evidence of learning gains.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX immersive training experiments could test whether controlled multisensory feedback changes attention, detection or information comprehension. The paper demonstrates a device and perceptual trade-offs, but operational training efficacy and long-term behavioral outcomes remain untested.
items.streamTitle: Wearable thermal passthrough added bidirectional cues to augmented reality
items.streamSummary: A palm-mounted warm/cool AR prototype supported thermal passthrough and dynamic cues in human tests; moving patterns improved immersion while fingertip-contact realism declined. Benefits for practitioner learning remain untested.
items.attribution: Watkins, Ghosh, Chow and Sarkar — Communications Engineering (AR wearable prototype and human tests, November 13)
